p: Hush! is a small tool to facilitate the sharing of .env files between developers without having to send them over Teams messages. It stores a secret for each of your .env files in a backend of your choice. Today that's the AWS Secrets Manager, and a project can spread its keys over several backends, for example over AWS regions, with a project setting.
With Hush!, you can finally store secrets like API tokens or passwords securely.

If you're unsure where to start using Hush!, we recommend the Installation guide. Or maybe you're feeling adventurous and would like to deploy your first secret or take a look at the commands Hush! offers.
AWS TypeScript
Github Repository
Documentation
To install Hush! for use in your project, install it like this:
yarn add -D hush-cli
npm install --dev hush-cli

Hush! keeps your secrets in a backend. Without a project setting, Hush! uses the AWS Secrets Manager in eu-central-1, so you can start right away. If your project needs another region, or keys spread over several backends, add a hush.config.json.
Commands that use the AWS backend need your AWS profile!

Hush! asks for an AWS profile only for commands that use the AWS backend. Without a project setting, that's every command Hush! provides. Before running one, select your AWS profile by running export AWS_PROFILE=your-profile-name in the shell. If you don't have an AWS profile for your command line yet, create one first using this guide. hush --help works without one.
After installing Hush! in your project, it's time to push your first secret to the AWS cloud!

To do so, it's important to select your AWS profile by running export AWS_PROFILE=your-profile-name in the shell. If you don't have an AWS profile for your command line yet, create one first using this guide.
Let's say you have a file called .env with the following content:
To make this file available to your fellow devs, you would run the following command:
yarn hush push my-first-hush ./.env
npx hush push my-first-hush ./.env
And that's it! Your secret file is now managed by Hush! in the AWS cloud. Your fellow devs can pull your changes by using the following command.
yarn hush pull my-first-hush ./.env
npx hush pull my-first-hush ./.env
Hush implements a version control system that ensures developers avoid conflicts from using different versions.
The version control system in Hush works on three levels:
Secret Versioning: Each secret in AWS SecretsManager is automatically versioned
Local Version Tracking: The .hushrc.json file tracks local versions
Conflict Prevention: Automatic checks before push operations
Hush automatically creates a .hushrc.json file in your project directory:

With a project setting that puts keys into other backends, a version is kept per store. A key in the default store (the AWS Secrets Manager in eu-central-1) has the entry name shown above, as in Hush! 4.1.0. A key in any other store gets the store added after an @:

So a key that moves to another backend starts with a version of its own there, and hush delete only removes the version of the store it deleted from. Warnings name the key and its store, not the entry name, for example for key hush-project-prod (AWS eu-west-1).
Note:
The .hushrc.json file is automatically updated during pull operations
The .hushrc.json file is used for conflict checking during push operations
With every hush push, the system goes through the following process:
Retrieve Current Version: Loads the current version from AWS SecretsManager
Check Local Version: Compares with the version in .hushrc.json
Conflict Detection: Warns about conflicts and prevents unintended overwrites
Version Increment: Automatically increases the version number by 1
Update Local Tracking: Updates the .hushrc.json file

c:
# Current version in AWS: 5
# Local version in .hushrc.json: 3

hush push my-project .env
# ⚠️ Warning: Current version (5) is greater than your current version (3)
# ⚠️ Use "hush pull" to pull the latest version first

# Solution 1: Pull latest version
hush pull my-project .env
# Local version is updated to 5

hush push my-project .env
# ✅ Success! Version is incremented to 6

# Solution 2: Use force flag (only when sure)
hush push my-project .env --force
# ⚠️ May overwrite newer changes!

To push the contents of a .env file, use the push command:
yarn hush push key envFile
So for example:
yarn hush push joern-prod ./.env
All keys get prefixed with hush- in the AWS SecretsManager to avoid namespace pollution.
You can also provide an optional parameter -m, --message to provide a sort of "commit message" for the current version of your secret.

Additionally, you can use the -f, --force parameter to bypass version checking. By default, Hush checks the local .hushrc.json file to ensure you're working with the latest version before pushing. If a version conflict is detected, you'll be prompted to run hush pull first. The --force flag skips this validation and allows you to push regardless of version conflicts.
To update the local contents of a .env file, use the pull command:
yarn hush pull key envFile
So for example:
yarn hush pull joern-prod ./.env
All keys get prefixed with hush- in the AWS SecretsManager to avoid namespace pollution.

If the newly pulled version of the .env file contains additions, changes, or deletions, your local .env file will not be overwritten. You can review those changes and then re-run the command with the --force flag.
This command outputs all contained secrets for one .env file managed by Hush!
This is useful for quickly seeing the contents of a .env file before pulling.

This command lists all Hush! secrets in the backend, without a project setting the AWS Secrets Manager in eu-central-1 with your current AWS profile. Secrets your profile can't read are listed as "No access".

If your project has a project setting with several backends, list shows one table per backend. Each table starts with a title row that names the backend and where it keeps its secrets, for example Backend: ireland (AWS eu-west-1). A backend that can't be listed shows the reason instead of a table; the other backends are still listed.
It displays the following fields for each secret:
Name
Last push message
Updated at
Secrets count
Please note that the Name has the "hush-" prefix attached to it.
Not illustrated in a gif to not expose secret information.
To grant another IAM user in the same AWS account access to your secret, use the grant command like this:
yarn hush grant joern-prod user-identifier
user-identifier has to be either an AWS ARN or a username for a user that shares an AWS account with you.
Not illustrated in a gif to not expose secret information.
To prevent another IAM user in the same AWS account from accessing your secret, use the revoke command like this:
yarn hush revoke joern-prod user-identifier
user-identifier has to be either an AWS ARN or a username for a user that shares an AWS account with you.
Please keep in mind that users with higher privileges than you might still be able to access the secrets.
To delete a secret, use the delete command:
yarn hush delete key
So for example:
yarn hush delete joern-prod
You can specify the --force parameter to force the deletion of the secret without scheduling the deletion for a later date.

A backend is the service where Hush! keeps your secrets. With a hush.config.json file, a project decides which backend holds which key. Every command reads it: push, pull, cat, grant, revoke and delete use the backend of the key you give them, and list shows all backends of the project.
You don't need this file. Without a hush.config.json, Hush! works as it always has: every key lives in the AWS Secrets Manager in eu-central-1, with the AWS profile from AWS_PROFILE.

Hush! looks for hush.config.json in the directory you run it in, usually the root of your project, next to .hushrc.json. It doesn't look in parent directories. Commit the file: it holds no secrets, and everyone on the project should use the same backends.
With this file, hush push shop-prod .env stores the secret hush-shop-prod in eu-west-1. Every other key, for example hush push blog-prod .env, goes to the default backend frankfurt in eu-central-1.

l: Every key has exactly one backend
p: A key belongs to the backend that keys names for it, otherwise to the default backend. Hush! never looks for a key in a second backend. If you move a key to another backend in keys, the secret doesn't move with it. To move it, for example shop-prod:
With the previous setting, run hush pull shop-prod .env, so your .env file holds the newest version.
Move the key in keys and run hush push shop-prod .env. This creates the secret in the new backend.
If you no longer need the old secret, delete it with the previous setting: hush delete shop-prod.

.hushrc.json keeps the version of a key per store, so the old and the new secret don't share a version, and deleting one doesn't touch the version of the other. Keys in the default AWS store (eu-central-1) keep the entry name they had in Hush! 4.1.0, like hush-shop-dev. Keys in any other store get the store added, like hush-shop-prod@AWS eu-west-1. See Version control.

With more than one backend, hush list shows one table per backend, in the order of backends (names that are whole numbers, like 2024, come first, as in every JSON object read by JavaScript). Each table starts with a title row like Backend: ireland (AWS eu-west-1). A table shows every Hush! secret in that backend, also secrets that keys assigns to another backend.
If a backend can't be listed, for example because no AWS profile is selected, list shows the reason instead of its table, still lists the other backends and ends with exit code 1.
With a single backend, list looks as it does without a project setting.
Hush! checks the file before every command and stops before it calls any backend. The message names the file and the field, for example:
A file that isn't valid JSON, a missing backends or default, an unknown type and a name in default or keys that isn't in backends are all mistakes.

A region that doesn't have the shape of an AWS region (words and a number, like eu-west-1, us-gov-west-1 or eusc-de-east-1) is a mistake. Hush! checks the shape, not a list of regions, so a new AWS region works right away.

Every store has one name. Two backends that point to the same store, like two AWS backends in the same region, are a mistake; a backend without region counts as eu-central-1. Otherwise list would show the same secrets twice.

Fields Hush! doesn't know are mistakes too, at the top level and in a backend. This keeps credentials out of the file: a field like secretAccessKey is refused, and Hush! doesn't repeat its value in the message.
hush --help still works with a broken file, so you can look up the commands while you fix it.

p: This page is for contributors who want Hush! to store secrets in another service. A new backend takes three steps: implement the backend interface, register the type so projects can choose it in hush.config.json, and pass the shared backend tests.

The commands' logic doesn't need to change: commands talk to a backend only through the interface. A few user texts in src/HushCommand.ts still name AWS (the warning of pull, the argument help of grant and revoke); check whether they fit your backend.

A lint rule keeps commands away from cloud code: files in src/commands/ may not import the packages and paths listed under no-restricted-imports in eslint.config.js (today @aws-sdk/*, @azure/*, the AWS backend folder and its requests). Add your service's SDK and your backend's folder to that list.
A readable name, e.g. AWS Secrets Manager.

An error message never contains the value of an entry. The message is shown to the user as it is, and secrets hold customer credentials.

Create a class in its own folder, for example src/backends/example/ExampleBackend.ts, that implements SecretBackend from src/backends/SecretBackend.ts. The AWS backend in src/backends/aws/ is a complete example.

Translate the service's errors into one of the kinds notFound, accessDenied, notSignedIn, invalidName, tooLarge, softDeleted, unknownFormat or other. Commands decide only by the kind, never by the service's own error names. src/backends/aws/toBackendError.ts shows how.

Schedules the entry for deletion, or deletes it for good with { force: true }. When it schedules, it reports the deletionDate, and reading the entry fails with softDeleted until then; the shared tests check both.

setupProblem() runs before a command uses the backend, so put checks like "is a profile or login there?" in it, not in the constructor. Hush! creates every backend of the project setting on each command, even ones the command doesn't use, and hush --help must work without any login.
The names of all entries that start with prefix.
Things every backend must get right:
What it does
write(name, value)
Projects choose a backend by its type in hush.config.json. Register yours in src/backends/backendTypes.ts:

With more than one settings type, settings is the union of all of them in every function of an entry (create, store and checkValues), so each of them narrows it to its own type, the AWS entry included (it does so already); otherwise yarn build fails.

required and optional list every field besides type that a backend of this type may have. Hush! refuses any other field, so no credentials can end up in the file: let the backend find them the way its service's tools do (a profile, an environment variable, a login), never as a field.

The project setting checks that every listed field is a non-empty string. A field of another kind (a number, a list) needs a change to that check in checkBackend in src/config/ProjectConfig.ts, which today refuses every field that isn't a string.

store names the store a backend points to, e.g. AWS eu-central-1. Two backends of the same type with the same store are refused, so give it everything that tells two stores apart and fill in the defaults of optional fields.
checkValues is optional and checks the values beyond "non-empty string", like the shape of the AWS region. It returns the field and the problem; the problem must not repeat the value.
Add the new type and its fields to the project setting page.

test/unit/backends/contract.test.ts holds the tests every backend has to pass: reading, writing, new versions, listing by prefix, deleting with and without force, the error kinds for missing and deleted entries, and that grantAccess and revokeAccess come as a pair. They don't try granting or revoking, so write your own tests for those. Add your backend to the backends list at the top of the file:
The unit tests must not call the real service: mock its client, as test/support/fakeSecretsManager.ts does for AWS. Use only made-up values in tests and examples.
